title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
summary: Union-Find answers one question near-instantly as edges arrive over time: are these two nodes in the same group? Union by rank and path compression together push it to almost O(1) per operation.

slides.markdown:
Union-Find (also called Disjoint Set Union, DSU) is built for exactly one question, answered efficiently as edges are added incrementally over time: **are these two elements in the same group right now?**

[connected-components-bipartite](connected-components-bipartite) answers this by re-running a full traversal — fine when the whole graph is known upfront, wasteful when edges arrive one at a time and you need an answer after each one. Union-Find's naive version is simple but slow on skewed input; two optimizations — union by rank/size and path compression — bring it down to a complexity so close to O(1) that it's routinely just called "almost constant time."

Every element starts as its own group, represented by a `parent` array where `parent[i] = i`. `find(i)` walks up parent pointers until it reaches an element that's its own parent — the **root**, which identifies the group. `union(a, b)` finds both roots and makes one point to the other, merging the groups.

The naive version's flaw: nothing controls which root ends up under which. A sequence of unions can produce a long chain — element 5 points to 4, which points to 3, which points to 2, which points to 1 — turning `find` into an O(n) walk in the worst case, no better than a linked list.

slides.sectionTitle: Union by rank/size: keep the tree shallow on purpose
slides.markdown:
Instead of always attaching one root under the other arbitrarily, track each tree's rank (an upper bound on its height) or size (its node count), and always attach the **smaller** tree under the **larger** one's root.

Why this bounds height: attaching a smaller tree under a larger one can only increase the resulting tree's height when the two trees were the same height to begin with — in that one case, height grows by exactly 1. This means height only grows logarithmically in the number of unions, giving O(log n) `find` even without the second optimization.

slides.sectionTitle: Path compression: flatten on every find
slides.markdown:
While `find(x)` walks up to the root, it's already discovered exactly which chain of parents `x` had to traverse. Path compression makes every node on that path point **directly to the root** once it's found, instead of leaving the chain intact for the next call to re-walk.

This doesn't change what the current `find` call returns, but it means the *next* `find` on any of those nodes is O(1) — a direct pointer to the root, no walk at all. The tree gets flatter every time it's queried, which is exactly the self-improving property that, combined with union by rank, produces the near-constant amortized bound.

slides.sectionTitle: A tall tree, before and after compression
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: two trees side by side; left labelled "before" shows a tall unbalanced chain, node E under D under C under B under A (root); right labelled "after path compression" shows the same 5 nodes but now B, C, D, E all point directly to A, flattening the structure to height 1 >>>

The picture is the whole payoff: one `find(E)` call pays the cost of walking the original chain once, but leaves every node on that path one hop from the root forever after — the next `find` on any of B, C, D, or E is now O(1).

With both optimizations, the amortized cost per operation is **O(α(n))**, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — a function that grows so slowly it's effectively a constant for any n that could ever exist in practice. α(n) stays below 5 even for n larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe.

This is why the combined structure is described as "almost O(1)" rather than truly O(1): the bound is technically not constant, but no realistic input will ever push α(n) high enough to matter. In practice, treat Union-Find operations as O(1) when reasoning about an algorithm's overall complexity.

slides.sectionTitle: Union-Find vs BFS/DFS: online vs offline
slides.markdown:
| | Union-Find | BFS/DFS components |
|---|---|---|
| Best fit | Edges arriving over time, frequent "same group?" queries | Whole graph known upfront, one-time component count |
| Per-operation cost | O(α(n)) amortized | Re-traversal needed for a fresh answer |
| Can it "un-union"? | No — merging is one-directional and permanent | Trivially recomputed if edges change |

Union-Find's one real limitation: it only supports merging groups, never splitting them back apart. If a problem needs to *remove* an edge and re-check connectivity, Union-Find alone doesn't handle it — that needs a different structure (or an offline trick like processing queries in reverse).

slides.sectionTitle: Cycle detection via "same set" before union
slides.markdown:
Union-Find gives a clean way to detect a cycle while building an undirected graph edge by edge: before unioning two nodes, check `find(a) == find(b)`. If they're already in the same set, adding this edge would connect two already-connected nodes — a cycle. If they're in different sets, union them and continue.

This is exactly the check embedded in the `union` method above (`if root_a == root_b: return False`) — a `union` call returning `False` is precisely "this edge would create a cycle," which is the mechanism Kruskal's algorithm depends on to skip cycle-forming edges.

Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting all edges by weight and adding each one greedily, skipping any edge that would close a cycle. Union-Find is precisely the mechanism that makes "would this edge close a cycle" a near-O(1) check instead of a full reachability search per candidate edge.

The pattern: for each edge `(u, v, w)` in weight order, call `union(u, v)` — if it returns `True` (they were in different sets), keep the edge as part of the MST; if it returns `False`, skip it. This is covered in depth in the minimum-spanning-trees topic later in this group.

A subtle bug: implementing union by rank but attaching the tree with the **higher** rank under the one with the **lower** rank — backwards from the intended rule. This doesn't produce wrong answers (the sets are still merged correctly), but it silently defeats the entire point of the optimization: the resulting tree can grow taller than necessary, degrading `find` back toward the naive O(n) worst case on adversarial input sequences.

The rule to double-check in code review: the smaller-rank root always ends up pointing to the larger-rank root, never the reverse — and skipping path compression is a related but separate mistake, since without it a chain built by many unions of similar-rank trees can still be O(log n) deep rather than O(1) via compression.
